claims.v: USAF pilot disappeared while performing an air defense intercept over Lake Superior
claims.quote: First Lieutenant Felix Eugene Moncla Jr. (October 21, 1926 – presumed dead November 23, 1953) was a United States Air Force (USAF) pilot who disappeared while performing an air defense intercept over Lake Superior in 1953.

claims.v: Moncla crashed into Lake Superior while tracking an off-course RCAF C-47
claims.quote: The USAF reported that Moncla had crashed into Lake Superior while tracking a Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) C-47 aircraft which was off course.

claims.v: the pilot of the Canadian aircraft did not know he was the subject of an interception
claims.quote: According to the report, the pilot of the Canadian aircraft did not know that he was the subject of an interception.

claims.v: Air Defense Command Ground Intercept radar operators identified an unusual target over Lake Superior, near the Soo Locks
claims.quote: On the evening of November 23, 1953, Air Defense Command Ground Intercept radar operators at Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, identified an unusual target over Lake Superior, near the Soo Locks.

claims.v: ground radar operators gave Moncla directions towards the object as he flew
claims.quote: Wilson had a difficult time tracking the object on the Scorpion's radar, so ground radar operators gave Moncla directions towards the object as he flew.

claims.v: Ground Control tracked the Scorpion and the unidentified object as two blips
claims.quote: Ground Control tracked the Scorpion and the unidentified object as two "blips" on the radar screen.
Ground Control tracked the Scorpion and the unidentified object as two "blips" on the radar screen.

claims.v: the two blips grew closer and closer until they seemed to merge
claims.quote: The two blips on the radar screen grew closer and closer until they seemed to merge.

claims.v: assumed Moncla had flown under or over the target and that two separate blips would reappear moments later
claims.quote: Assuming that Moncla had flown either under or over the target, Ground Control anticipated that moments later, the Scorpion and the object would again appear as two separate blips.

claims.v: feared the two objects had struck one another; the single blip continued on its previous course
claims.quote: There was a fear that the two objects had struck one another, but the single blip continued on its previous course.

claims.v: attempts to contact Moncla via radio were without success
claims.quote: Attempts were made to contact Moncla via radio, but without success.

claims.v: USAF and RCAF search and rescue operation failed to find any trace of the plane or its pilots
claims.quote: A search and rescue operation by both the USAF and the Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) was quickly mounted, but failed to find any trace of the plane or its pilots.

claims.v: weather conditions were a factor in hampering the search
claims.quote: Weather conditions were a factor in hampering the search.

claims.v: 8,000 feet
claims.quote: The F-89 was flying at an elevation of 8,000 feet when it merged with the other aircraft, as was expected in an interception.

claims.v: pilot of another F-89 sent on the search believed he heard a brief radio transmission from the pilot about forty minutes after the plane disappeared
claims.quote: Although efforts to contact the crew on radio were unsuccessful, the pilot of another F-89 sent on the search stated in testimony to the accident board that he believed that he had heard a brief radio transmission from the pilot about forty minutes after the plane disappeared.

claims.v: about forty minutes after the plane disappeared
